newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends lower vs. German mark, up against yen.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends lower vs. German mark, up against yen.

text.p: The dollar slipped against the German mark Tuesday as renewed fears that the Bundesbank might raise interest rates next week to strengthen its battered currency brought an end to an early rally.
But the dollar eked out slim gains against the Japanese yen after a spate of nervous buying by traders who had bet the U.S. currency would fall.
The dollar jumped about half a pfennig after the Bundesbank held a key interest rate steady early Tuesday.
The dollar topped 1.87 marks at one point, its highest since Friday's nerve-wracking slide dragged it down nearly 3 percent from an eight-year high set a week ago.
But it retreated later in the day, as worries resurfaced that the German central bank might boost rates next week upon its return from summer recess.
The dollar closed at 1.8630 marks, down from 1.8640 Monday in New York trading.
Intense speculation that the German central bank would allow interest rates to move higher in order to curb the mark's steady decline this year had weighed on the dollar recently.

But views that Germany needs a weak currency to keep its export-driven economy competitive before Europe launches its single currency in 1999 has renewed buying interest in the U.S. currency. Higher interest rates tend to raise the value of a currency by boosting the price of assets denominated in that currency.
Although the outlook for German interest rates is unclear, the strong U.S. economy and relatively high interest rates are still working in favour of the dollar, analysts said.

"It's definitely cautious, but I think we had a bit of a correction and you still have to look to buy on dips," said Lizbeth Goldberg, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Bayerische Hypotheken und Weschelsbank.
The dollar ended at 116.28 yen, up from 116.18 Monday, after failing to hold onto gains scored early in the session.

The U.S. currency rose above 116.50 yen at one point, prompting a rush by investors who had bet on a decline to buy the U.S. currency to cover short positions. But the advance faltered below the widely watched 117-yen level.
Speculators often make bets on a weaker dollar by selling the currency short, hoping to buy it back at a cheaper price for a profit.
Analysts said the dollar is unlikely to make a big move higher before the release over the next few days of key data on inflation and retail sales.
A strong showing on the retail sales figures in particular could fan fears that the Federal Reserve would be forced to hike interest rates to head off inflation.

"That should put the scare back in the bond market, and I think dollar bulls probably want to see the bond market stabilise before they get aggressive about buying," said David Gilmore, a partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics, a Connecticut consulting firm.
In other trade, the dollar ended unchanged at 1.5263 Swiss francs and closed at Canadian $1.3935, compared with C$1.3934 Monday. The pound fell to $1.5788 from $1.5900.
